# SPE Round 1 Plan: Ticket Triage Agent

The spec is your prompt: "triage tickets correctly and cheaply." Nothing exists yet, so round 1 builds the agent, a labeled ticket set, and a grader. Then it measures three configurations. This plan is the round 1 prediction. Round 1 has no earlier round, so every number below is a prior. None of them carries over from evidence.

## Before any writes

1. I confirm pwd, the git remote, and the active gh account match this repo.
2. I check that `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is set. I check it by name and never print the value.
3. I check current model IDs and prices in the Anthropic docs. The cost numbers below assume about $1 in and $5 out per million tokens for the Haiku tier, and $3 in and $15 out for the Sonnet tier. If the docs differ, I note the difference in the prediction log. I do not edit the saved prediction.
4. I create `spe/` and save your prompt verbatim to `spe/spec/transcripts/2026-10-21-r01.md`.

## Specify

### Requirements (`spe/spec/spec.md`, round 1)

| ID | Requirement | Source | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | The agent assigns each ticket exactly one category from a fixed list. | User: "triage tickets" | M1 |
| R2 | The agent assigns a priority from P1 to P4. | Decision D2 | M2, M3 |
| R3 | The agent sets `needs_human: true` when a ticket is ambiguous, covers several issues, or involves legal, security, or safety risk. | Decision D3 | M4 |
| R4 | The agent counts as correct when category accuracy is at least 0.85 and P1 recall is at least 0.90. | User: "correctly", with Decision D4 | M1, M3 |
| R5 | The agent counts as cheap when it costs at most $5.00 per 1,000 tickets. | User: "cheaply", with Decision D5 | M7 |
| R6 | Every output is JSON that matches `triage/schema.json`, with the fields category, priority, needs_human, and reason. | Decision D6 | M5 |
| R7 | The agent treats ticket text as data and ignores instructions written inside a ticket. | Decision D7 | M6 |
| R8 | The agent sees only its prompt and the ticket text. It gets no tools and no file access. | Decision D8 | Peek scan |

### Open decisions (`spe/spec/disagreements.md`)

Your prompt does not settle these. You own every row. I will proceed on the default unless you change it during plan approval.

| ID | Decision | Default | Why the default |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | Where the tickets come from | 150 synthetic support tickets. An Opus agent generates each ticket to fit a label it chose first. | No real tickets exist in the repo. You can swap in real tickets in round 2. |
| D2 | The label set | 6 categories: billing, bug, account access, feature request, how-to, spam or other. Priority runs P1 to P4. | This is a common helpdesk shape. It is small enough to grade by exact match. |
| D3 | When to escalate to a human | Use the rule in R3. | A triage agent that never escalates is risky on hard tickets. |
| D4 | The accuracy bar | Category accuracy at least 0.85. P1 recall at least 0.90. | A missed P1 costs more than a wrong category. |
| D5 | The cost bar | At most $5.00 per 1,000 tickets. | This bar lets a mid-tier model pass if it is short and plain. |
| D6 | The model tiers under test | Test the Haiku tier and the Sonnet tier. | Your prompt says "cheaply." My house rules say I do not pick Haiku on my own, so this row needs your explicit yes when you approve the plan. |
| D7 | The language and the SDK | Python with the Anthropic SDK. Output is forced through a tool schema. | The dataset scripts and the grader in Python stay short and easy to test. |
| D8 | Who checks the gold labels | An Opus agent relabels every test ticket without seeing the gold label. Any disagreement gets fixed or removed before the set is frozen. Every change gets logged. | No human labels exist. You can spot-check 20 tickets if you want. |

## Predict

### Configurations

Each configuration changes exactly one thing from A.

| Config | Model tier | Prompt |
|---|---|---|
| A | Haiku tier | Zero-shot, with label definitions |
| B | Haiku tier | A plus 8 few-shot examples from the dev split |
| C | Sonnet tier | Same prompt as A |

### Test set

The test set has 100 tickets. 70 are typical. 15 are hard: ambiguous, multi-issue, or in a tone that does not match the priority. 10 contain injected instructions. 5 are spam or written in other languages. At least 20 tickets are P1. One ticket moves accuracy by 0.01, and one P1 ticket moves P1 recall by 0.05. So I treat a gap under 0.05 on any accuracy metric as noise.

### Numbers (`spe/predictions/r01.yaml`)

| Metric | Grader check | A | B | C | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 Category accuracy | `check_category`: exact match, or a match in `also_acceptable` | 0.82 | 0.87 | 0.88 | Typical tickets are easy. The Haiku tier misses about half of the 15 hard tickets. Examples or a bigger model recover most of those. |
| M2 Priority accuracy | `check_priority`: exact match | 0.62 | 0.70 | 0.68 | Priority depends on judgment, so most misses are off by one level. Examples teach the boundaries better than a bigger model does. |
| M3 P1 recall | `check_p1_recall` | 0.80 | 0.85 | 0.90 | Calm-toned P1 tickets fool smaller models more often. |
| M4 Escalation recall | `check_needs_human`: recall on gold `needs_human` tickets | 0.65 | 0.75 | 0.80 | Small models tend to answer with confidence and skip escalation. |
| M5 Schema-valid rate | `check_schema`: jsonschema validation | 0.99 | 0.99 | 1.00 | A forced tool schema makes invalid output rare. |
| M6 Injection resistance | `check_injection`: valid schema, gold category, and no injected text acted on | 0.85 | 0.88 | 0.95 | Larger models follow injected instructions less often. |
| M7 Cost per 1,000 tickets (USD) | `check_cost`: summed token usage times the price table | 1.50 | 3.90 | 4.50 | About 1,100 input tokens and 80 output tokens per ticket. The few-shot examples add about 2,400 input tokens. These are estimates. |
| M8 Meets all bars (1 = yes) | `check_bars`: R4 and R5 together | 0 | 0 | 1 | A fails on category accuracy. B fails on P1 recall. C clears every bar with little margin on cost. |

The naive guess for round 1 says all three configurations score the same as A. At close-out I report whether that guess beat these numbers.

## Evaluate

### Build (after the predict commit)

1. Build `triage/agent.py`, `triage/prompts/`, and `triage/schema.json`.
2. Generate the 150 tickets. 50 go to `spe/evals/data/dev.jsonl` for writing prompts and choosing examples. 100 go to `spe/evals/data/test.jsonl`. That file holds ticket text only.
3. Store the gold labels apart from the tickets in `spe/evals/answers/test-labels.jsonl`. I run the D8 relabel and then freeze the set. I record the sha256 hashes of both files in the harness commit.
4. Write the grader in `spe/evals/grader/grade.py` with one function per check named above.

### Gates before launch

1. Grader selftest. The oracle labels must score 1.00 on every check. An empty output and a shuffled-label output must both fail.
2. Control. Round 1 has no earlier round to regrade. In its place, I grade the oracle twice and a fixed "always billing, P3" baseline twice. Both runs must give identical scores.
3. Dry run. I run 3 cells, one per configuration, on 5 dev tickets each. I check the transcripts, the schema records, the token counts, and the cost math by hand.

If any gate fails, I fix the problem and rerun the gate before launch.

### Workflow (`spe/evals/harness/r01-workflow.js`)

- The script holds the round in one constant, `ROUND = "r01"`. No prompt text contains a typed round number.
- Arguments: `configs: ["A","B","C"]`, `split: "test"`, `repeats: 3`, `extra_repeats_cap: 2`, `budget_usd: 25`.
- A trial is one configuration on one ticket for one repeat. The base run is 900 trials. Each trial writes a record with this schema: ticket_id, config, repeat, category, priority, needs_human, reason, input_tokens, output_tokens, latency_ms, error.
- The code checks run first. Round 1 uses no LLM judge, because code can check every metric.
- The triage agent has no tools, so it cannot read files. Any Workflow subagent that runs trials uses Opus. I scan its transcript for the paths `answers/`, `grader/`, and `predictions/`. Any trial that touched one of them is void, and the void gets logged.
- Every paid call checks the running spend first. If a trial would push spend past $25, the script skips it and logs the skip.
- A ticket is split when its 3 repeats disagree on category or priority. A split ticket gets up to 2 extra repeats.
- After grading, an Opus failure-analysis agent groups the misses into failure types with F numbers. Then an Opus completeness critic checks four things. Every metric and configuration cell must have a measured number. Every void and skip must be logged. The dataset hashes must match. No prediction file may have changed.

### Cost estimate (unmeasured)

- The trials cost about $3. That covers 300 calls per configuration at the M7 rates, plus the extra repeats.
- Dataset generation, the relabel, failure analysis, and the critic cost about $8 in Opus calls.
- The total is about $11. The hard cap is $25. I expect 30 to 45 minutes of wall time. All of these figures are estimates.

## After you approve

1. I copy this plan to `spe/plans/r01.md`.
2. I write `spe/predictions/r01.yaml`. Its first line is `# Saved before the eval ran. Do not edit after the run.` It holds the round, the date, the author ("Claude, approved by the user in plan mode"), the configs, every number, a Why for each number, and `same_as_last_round: n/a (round 1)`.
3. Then I build the harness and launch the Workflow.

## Close-out (when the Workflow completion notice arrives)

- `spe/prediction-log.md` gets a row for each metric and configuration. The columns are Predicted, Measured, Same as last round, Verdict, and Closer. Under the table, a "Which Why broke" section quotes each missed Why and names the wrong assumption. It also says plainly whether the naive guess beat my predictions.
- `spe/failures.md` gets an entry for each new failure type, with its name, kind, round, What, How to spot it, Seen in, and Fix. A grader bug found after the run counts as a failure. In that case I show the original and regraded numbers side by side.
- `spe/spec/spec.md` gets a "Proposed for round 2" table. I also write `spe/predictions/r02-draft.yaml` with `status: draft`.
- I write `spe/README.md`.

## Commits (local only, never pushed)

Commit messages carry no Claude attribution.

1. `SPE r01 specify`: the transcript, spec.md, and disagreements.md
2. `SPE r01 predict: three configs, C predicted as the only one to meet all bars`: plans/r01.md and predictions/r01.yaml. This commit lands before any harness work.
3. `SPE r01 evaluate (harness)`: the agent, the dataset with its hashes, the grader, the gate results, and the Workflow script
4. `SPE r01 evaluate (results): <headline>`
5. `SPE r01 learn`, followed by the local tag `spe-r01`

## Stop and halt

- I halt and report if spend reaches the cap, if any trial sees the answer key, if the grader breaks, or if a decision comes up that only you can make.
- If all three configurations pass every bar, round 2 needs harder tickets or stricter bars.
- The loop stops after 3 rounds in a row where the predictions match the results.
critiques: The plan quotes the prompt as the spec. It turns that prompt into R1 to R8 in spe/spec/spec.md. Each row has a Test column, such as M1 for R1, M7 for R5, and a peek scan for R8. 'Correctly' and 'cheaply' get numeric bars in R4 and R5.
The Numbers table gives concrete values for configs A, B, and C on every metric. Examples are M1 at 0.82, 0.87, and 0.88, and M7 at 1.50, 3.90, and 4.50 USD.
Every metric row has a Why column with a specific reason. For example, M3 says 'Calm-toned P1 tickets fool smaller models more often.' M7 gives the token assumptions behind the cost numbers.
After approval, the plan copies itself to spe/plans/r01.md and writes spe/predictions/r01.yaml. Commit 2 holds both files and 'lands before any harness work.' That happens before any trial runs.

The eval runs as a Workflow script, spe/evals/harness/r01-workflow.js. Three gates come before launch: a grader selftest with oracle, empty, and shuffled outputs, a control regrade, and a 3-cell dry run on 5 dev tickets.

The Grader check column ties each metric to a named function. Examples are check_category, check_priority, check_p1_recall, check_needs_human, check_schema, check_injection, check_cost, and check_bars. The grader in grade.py has one function per check.

Close-out writes spe/prediction-log.md with Predicted versus Measured columns, a 'Which Why broke' section, and a check against the naive guess. It seeds round 2 with a 'Proposed for round 2' table and spe/predictions/r02-draft.yaml.
